lesson_scope: Triangles in coordinate geometry: right-angled triangles and gradient tests, isosceles triangles and distance equality, equilateral triangle vertex construction, altitudes and foot of perpendicular, triangle area calculations, and circumcircle centre of right-angled triangles.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: proving a right angle at a triangle vertex using perpendicular gradients.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of proving right-angled triangle by perpendicular gradients.

hints: Calculate the gradient of line segment $AB$: $m_{AB} = \dfrac{5 - 1}{4 - 1}$.
Calculate the gradient of line segment $BC$: $m_{BC} = \dfrac{8 - 5}{0 - 4}$.
Multiply the two gradients: show that $m_{AB} \times m_{BC} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{4}\right) = -1$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the gradients of segments $AB$ and $BC$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{5 - 1}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{3}$$
$$m_{BC} = \dfrac{8 - 5}{0 - 4} = \dfrac{3}{-4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}$$

Multiply the two gradients to test for perpendicularity:
$$m_{AB} \times m_{BC} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{4}\right) = -1$$
Since their gradient product is $-1$, $AB \perp BC$, so triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: calculating the area of a right-angled triangle from coordinate side lengths.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of calculating right-angled triangle area.

hints: Since the right angle is at $Q$, the base and height are the lengths of $PQ$ and $QR$.
Apply the area formula: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times PQ \times QR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 8 = 16$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the lengths of the two perpendicular sides meeting at $Q$:
$$PQ = \sqrt{(6 - 2)^2 + (3 - 3)^2} = 4$$
$$QR = \sqrt{(6 - 6)^2 + (11 - 3)^2} = 8$$

Calculate the area of the right-angled triangle:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times PQ \times QR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 8 = 16$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: proving a triangle is isosceles by calculating equal side lengths.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of proving an isosceles triangle by side lengths.

hints: Show that $AB = BC = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$, establishing that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the distance formula to find side lengths $AB$ and $BC$:
$$AB = \sqrt{(5 - 1)^2 + (4 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 4} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$$
$$BC = \sqrt{(3 - 5)^2 + (8 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$$

Conclude the isosceles property:
$$AB = BC = 2\sqrt{5}$$
Since two side lengths are equal, triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

ai_rubric.observable: Shows $AB = BC = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$ and concludes triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: finding base midpoint and altitude length in an isosceles triangle.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of evaluating isosceles base midpoint and altitude.

hints: Find the midpoint $M$ of base $BC$ by averaging coordinates of $B(-2, 1)$ and $C(6, 1)$.
Use the distance formula between vertex $A(2, 7)$ and midpoint $M(2, 1)$ to find $AM = 7 - 1 = 6$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the midpoint $M$ of base $BC$:
$$M = \left(\dfrac{-2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{4}{2}, \dfrac{2}{2}\right) = (2, 1)$$

Calculate the length of the altitude $AM$:
$$AM = \sqrt{(2 - 2)^2 + (7 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{0^2 + 6^2} = 6$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: calculating the area of a triangle from base length and perpendicular height.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of calculating triangle area using base and height.

hints: Since $B(-3, 2)$ and $C(5, 2)$ lie on the horizontal line $y = 2$, the base length is $BC = 5 - (-3) = 8$.
The perpendicular height is the vertical distance from $A(1, 8)$ down to $y = 2$, giving $h = 8 - 2 = 6$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the horizontal base length $BC$ and the perpendicular height from $A$:
$$BC = |5 - (-3)| = 8$$
$$\text{Height } h = |8 - 2| = 6$$

Calculate the area of triangle $ABC$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies horizontal base length $BC = 5 - (-3) = 8$ and perpendicular height $h = 8 - 2 = 6$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: finding an unknown coordinate parameter from a right-angled triangle condition.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving for unknown parameter in a right-angled triangle.

hints: Since $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, the perpendicular gradient of $BC$ is $m_{BC} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate gradient $m_{AB}$ and find the perpendicular gradient $m_{BC}$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{6 - 0}{3 - 0} = 2$$
$$m_{BC} = -\dfrac{1}{m_{AB}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$

Set up the gradient formula for $BC$ and solve for $k$:
$$m_{BC} = \dfrac{0 - 6}{k - 3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\dfrac{-6}{k - 3} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \implies k - 3 = 12 \implies k = 15$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: proving a triangle is right-angled using perpendicular gradients and evaluating its area from side lengths.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proving right-angled triangle by computing gradients and testing m1*m2 = -1.

hints: Multiply the two gradients: $m_{PQ} \times m_{QR} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right) = -1 \implies \angle PQR = 90^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the gradients of segments $PQ$ and $QR$:
$$m_{PQ} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$m_{QR} = \dfrac{9 - 5}{2 - 5} = \dfrac{4}{-3} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$$

Multiply the two gradients:
$$m_{PQ} \times m_{QR} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right) = -1$$
Since $m_{PQ} \times m_{QR} = -1$, the line segments $PQ$ and $QR$ are perpendicular, hence triangle $PQR$ is right-angled at $Q$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Calculating area of right-angled triangle from leg lengths.

hints: Since the triangle is right-angled at $Q$, $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times PQ \times QR$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the lengths of the two legs $PQ$ and $QR$:
$$PQ = \sqrt{(5 - 1)^2 + (5 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = \sqrt{25} = 5$$
$$QR = \sqrt{(2 - 5)^2 + (9 - 5)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5$$

Calculate the area of the right-angled triangle:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times PQ \times QR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 5 = 12.5$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: expressing squared distances algebraically in terms of unknown parameter $p$ and equating them for an isosceles triangle.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Expressing squared distances algebraically in terms of a coordinate parameter.

hints: Expand both expressions fully: $AC^2 = p^2 + 2p + 26$ and $BC^2 = p^2 - 14p + 58$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the squared distance formula to $AC$:
$$AC^2 = (p - (-1))^2 + (8 - 3)^2 = (p + 1)^2 + 5^2 = p^2 + 2p + 1 + 25 = p^2 + 2p + 26$$

Apply the squared distance formula to $BC$:
$$BC^2 = (p - 7)^2 + (8 - 5)^2 = (p - 7)^2 + 3^2 = p^2 - 14p + 49 + 9 = p^2 - 14p + 58$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Equating squared distances to solve for an unknown coordinate parameter.

hints: Cancel $p^2$ from both sides to form a linear equation in $p$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the expressions for $AC^2$ and $BC^2$:
$$p^2 + 2p + 26 = p^2 - 14p + 58$$

Cancel $p^2$ and collect like terms:
$$2p + 14p = 58 - 26$$
$$16p = 32 \implies p = 2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Equates $p^2 + 2p + 26 = p^2 - 14p + 58$ and eliminates quadratic terms.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: setting up perpendicular gradients involving a parameter $k$ to derive a quadratic equation and finding multiple vertex positions.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Forming quadratic parameter equation from right-angle gradient condition.

hints: The right-angle condition at $C$ requires $m_{AC} \times m_{BC} = -1$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the gradients of $AC$ and $BC$ in terms of $k$:
$$m_{AC} = \dfrac{k - (-2)}{2k - 3} = \dfrac{k + 2}{2k - 3}$$
$$m_{BC} = \dfrac{k - 4}{2k - 11}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Expresses gradients $m_{AC} = \dfrac{k + 2}{2k - 3}$ and $m_{BC} = \dfrac{k - 4}{2k - 11}$, and sets $m_{AC} \times m_{BC} = -1$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Solving quadratic equation to determine possible coordinates of vertex.

hints: Obtain the two values of $k$: $k = 1$ and $k = 5$.
Substitute each $k$ into $(2k, k)$ to get the coordinates of $C$: $C(2, 1)$ and $C(10, 5)$.

walkthrough.text:
Factorize the quadratic equation:
$$k^2 - 6k + 5 = 0 \implies (k - 1)(k - 5) = 0$$
$$k = 1 \quad \text{or} \quad k = 5$$

Substitute each value of $k$ into $C(2k, k)$:
$$\text{When } k = 1: C = (2(1), 1) = (2, 1)$$
$$\text{When } k = 5: C = (2(5), 5) = (10, 5)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Substitutes into $(2k, k)$ to obtain $C(2, 1)$ and $C(10, 5)$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: verifying isosceles side lengths, finding base midpoint, evaluating perpendicular altitude length, and computing area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proving isosceles triangle by distance formula and finding base midpoint.

hints: Since $AB = AC = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}$, $ABC$ is isosceles with base $BC$. Midpoint $M = \left(\dfrac{5 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{6 - 6}{2}\right) = (3, 0)$.

walkthrough.text:
Since $AB = AC = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}$, triangle $ABC$ is isosceles. Find the midpoint $M$ of base $BC$:
$$M = \left(\dfrac{5 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{6 + (-6)}{2}\right) = (3, 0)$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Calculating altitude length from vertex to base midpoint and finding area.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the length of the altitude $AM$ from $A(-3, 2)$ to $M(3, 0)$:
$$AM = \sqrt{(3 - (-3))^2 + (0 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 4} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}$$

Calculate the base length $BC$ and the area of triangle $ABC$:
$$BC = \sqrt{(1 - 5)^2 + (-6 - 6)^2} = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-12)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 144} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10}$$
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times BC \times AM = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4\sqrt{10} \times 2\sqrt{10} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 10 = 40$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: constructing equilateral triangle vertex coordinates from side length geometry and calculating exact surd area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding coordinates of third vertex in an equilateral triangle.

hints: Find the side length: $PQ = |4 - (-2)| = 6$. Midpoint of base is $M(1, 0)$.
In an equilateral triangle of side $s = 6$, the height is $h = s \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}$.
Since $R$ lies directly above $M(1, 0)$, its coordinates are $R(1, 3\sqrt{3})$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the side length and midpoint of base $PQ$:
$$PQ = |4 - (-2)| = 6$$
$$M = \left(\dfrac{-2 + 4}{2}, 0\right) = (1, 0)$$

Calculate the altitude $h$ of the equilateral triangle and state coordinates of $R$:
$$h = \sqrt{6^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{36 - 9} = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}$$
Since $R$ lies above the $x$-axis on the perpendicular line $x = 1$, $R = (1, 3\sqrt{3})$.

ai_rubric.observable: Finds midpoint of base $M(1, 0)$ and uses side length $6$ to find altitude $h = 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}$ (or solves $(x+2)^2+y^2=36$ and $(x-4)^2+y^2=36$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Calculating exact surd area of an equilateral triangle.

hints: Use the standard triangle area formula: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.
Simplify to get the exact area $9\sqrt{3}$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the area formula with base $PQ = 6$ and altitude $h = 3\sqrt{3}$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times PQ \times h = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 3\sqrt{3}$$

Simplify the surd expression:
$$\text{Area} = 3 \times 3\sqrt{3} = 9\sqrt{3}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: constructing base line equation and perpendicular altitude line, finding their simultaneous intersection (foot of perpendicular), and computing triangle area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding equations of base line and perpendicular altitude line.

hints: The altitude through $C(1, 7)$ has perpendicular gradient $-2$: $y - 7 = -2(x - 1) \implies 2x + y = 9$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the gradient of line $AB$ and write its equation:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{5 - (-1)} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$y - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x - (-1)) \implies 2(y - 1) = x + 1 \implies x - 2y + 3 = 0$$
$$y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{3}{2}$$

Determine the perpendicular gradient and write the altitude equation through $C(1, 7)$:
$$m_{\text{alt}} = -\dfrac{1}{1/2} = -2$$
$$y - 7 = -2(x - 1) \implies y - 7 = -2x + 2 \implies 2x + y = 9$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates gradient $m_{AB} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{5 - (-1)} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and writes line equation $y - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x + 1)$.
Forms altitude through $C(1, 7)$ with perpendicular gradient $-2$ to obtain $2x + y = 9$ (or $y = -2x + 9$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding foot of perpendicular by simultaneous equations and calculating area.

hints: Solve the simultaneous equations $x - 2y + 3 = 0$ and $2x + y = 9$.
Calculate base $AB = \sqrt{6^2 + 3^2} = 3\sqrt{5}$ and altitude $CD = \sqrt{(3-1)^2 + (3-7)^2} = 2\sqrt{5}$, then area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{5})(2\sqrt{5}) = 15$.

walkthrough.text:
Solve the simultaneous equations for the foot of the perpendicular $D$:
$$\text{From altitude: } y = 9 - 2x$$
$$\text{Substitute into line } AB: x - 2(9 - 2x) + 3 = 0$$
$$x - 18 + 4x + 3 = 0 \implies 5x = 15 \implies x = 3$$
$$y = 9 - 2(3) = 3 \implies D(3, 3)$$

Calculate the lengths of base $AB$ and altitude $CD$:
$$AB = \sqrt{(5 - (-1))^2 + (4 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{36 + 9} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$$
$$CD = \sqrt{(3 - 1)^2 + (3 - 7)^2} = \sqrt{2^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$$
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AB \times CD = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3\sqrt{5} \times 2\sqrt{5} = 15$$

ai_rubric.observable: Solves simultaneous equations $x - 2y + 3 = 0$ and $2x + y = 9$ to obtain $D(3, 3)$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: parameter determination for right-angled triangle, calculating exact area, and identifying the circumcentre as the hypotenuse midpoint.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proving parameter value from right angle condition at vertex.

hints: Since $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, the perpendicular gradient of $BC$ must be $m_{BC} = -1$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate gradient $m_{AB}$ and find the perpendicular gradient $m_{BC}$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{6 - 1}{2 - (-3)} = \dfrac{5}{5} = 1$$
$$m_{BC} = -\dfrac{1}{m_{AB}} = -1$$

Set up the gradient of $BC$ with $B(2, 6)$ and $C(k, 1)$:
$$m_{BC} = \dfrac{1 - 6}{k - 2} = \dfrac{-5}{k - 2}$$
$$\dfrac{-5}{k - 2} = -1 \implies k - 2 = 5 \implies k = 7$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Calculating area of right-angled isosceles triangle and finding circumcentre as hypotenuse midpoint.

hints: In any right-angled triangle, the circumcentre (centre of the circumscribing circle) is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AC$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the lengths of the perpendicular legs $AB$ and $BC$ using $k = 7$:
$$AB = \sqrt{(2 - (-3))^2 + (6 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$$
$$BC = \sqrt{(7 - 2)^2 + (1 - 6)^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$$

Calculate the area of right-angled triangle $ABC$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AB \times BC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5\sqrt{2} \times 5\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50 = 25$$

Determine the circumcentre: by Thales's theorem, the hypotenuse $AC$ of a right-angled triangle is a diameter of its circumcircle, so the centre is the midpoint of $AC$:
$$\text{Centre } M = \left(\dfrac{-3 + 7}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{4}{2}, \dfrac{2}{2}\right) = (2, 1)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies that the circumcentre of a right-angled triangle is the midpoint of its hypotenuse $AC$.
Calculates midpoint of $AC$ with $A(-3, 1)$ and $C(7, 1)$ as $M\left(\dfrac{-3 + 7}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 1}{2}\right) = (2, 1)$.
